title: The Motorola-MOS Axis II: The MOS Technology 6502, Zero Page & the Home-Computer Revolution (1975–1986)
summary: Part 2 of the Motorola-MOS Axis Quest Arc offers a relaxed, generalist-friendly 100-question journey through the MOS Technology 6502 (1975–1986), building directly on the Motorola 6800 module while explaining every silicon, addressing, and system concept from first principles. From Chuck Peddle and Bill Mensch's 25-dollar WESCON bombshell, depletion-mode NMOS wafer yield, little-endian pipelining, Zero Page pseudo-registers, indirect addressing modes, and the indirect JMP wraparound bug to the Apple II, Commodore 64, Atari 2600, Atari 800, BBC Micro, and Nintendo NES, learners trace how one minimalist chip democratized computing and planted the seed of ARM.
topic_prompt: Teach the MOS Technology 6502 (1975–1986) from first principles at a relaxed, generalist-friendly conversational pace (10 sections, 50 chunks, ~16 concepts), building directly on the Motorola 6800 module. Begin with the human and business drama: Chuck Peddle, Bill Mensch, and their team breaking away from Motorola in 1974 over high chip pricing, the September 1975 WESCON 25-dollar bombshell (jars of 6501 and 6502 chips undercutting rivals by nearly an order of magnitude), and Motorola's lawsuit that retired the pin-compatible 6501 while leaving the 6502—with its on-chip clock generator—free to reshape computing. Demystify the silicon economics that made a 25-dollar microprocessor profitable: its minimalist 3,510-transistor depletion-mode NMOS design, compact hand-drawn die, and optical mask-defect repair that dramatically boosted wafer yield. Explain little-endian byte order and the 6502's 2-stage fetch/execute overlap from first principles, showing why fetching the low address byte first let a 1 MHz 6502 perform address math while reading the high byte and rival higher-clocked competitors. Unpack the lean register model (A accumulator, 8-bit X and Y index registers, 8-bit stack pointer) and how the 256-byte Zero Page (0x0000–0x00FF) acted as a fast bank of pseudo-registers to make up for sparse on-chip registers. Teach the two signature Zero Page indirect addressing modes intuitively with concrete analogies: indexed indirect (zp,X) for picking from a table of pointers, versus indirect indexed (zp),Y for walking through arrays and screen rows. Examine the fixed Page-1 hardware stack (0x0100–0x01FF) and the famous indirect JMP page-boundary wraparound bug (jumping through an address ending in hex xxFF—such as 0x02FF—fetches the high byte from 0x0200 instead of 0x0300). Conclude with the vibrant software culture across six landmark 6502 platforms: the Apple II (Wozniak's cost-driven architecture and VisiCalc), Commodore PET and Commodore 64 (the 6510 variant with its built-in I/O port for memory bank switching), the Atari 2600 (cost-cut 28-pin 6507 and cycle-counted 'racing the beam' scanline programming), the Atari 800 (paired with ANTIC/GTIA/POKEY coprocessors), the 2 MHz Acorn BBC Micro (BBC BASIC and the seed of ARM), and the Nintendo Famicom/NES (custom Ricoh 2A03 omitting BCD hardware while adding on-chip audio).

sections.title: 1. The Motorola Breakaway & the 25-Dollar WESCON Bombshell (1974–1975)
sections.summary: Follow Chuck Peddle, Bill Mensch, and their colleagues as they leave Motorola's 6800 team in 1974 to build a radically affordable microprocessor at MOS Technology, stun the September 1975 WESCON trade show with jars of 6501 and 6502 chips priced nearly an order of magnitude below rivals, and survive Motorola's lawsuit that retired the pin-compatible 6501 while sparing the 6502 and its built-in on-chip clock generator.

chunks.title: Walkout Over a 25-Dollar Dream
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1974, a **microprocessor**—a tiny silicon chip housing the central computing brain of a machine—was still priced like luxury industrial gear. Motorola had just finished its impressive 6800 microprocessor, selling early evaluation kits and chips for roughly 175 to 300 dollars apiece. Yet one member of Motorola's own 6800 design team, an outspoken engineer named **Chuck Peddle**, kept hearing a different message on customer visits. Makers of cash registers, office terminals, and everyday appliances loved what microprocessors could do, but laughed at triple-digit chip prices.

Peddle returned to Motorola management with an audacious pitch: design a stripped-down microprocessor selling for just 25 dollars and watch sales explode across millions of consumer devices. Motorola executives flatly rejected the plan, worried that an ultra-cheap chip would cannibalize their profitable 6800 lineup. Convinced the future belonged to affordable silicon, Peddle, circuit designer **Bill Mensch**, and six fellow Motorola engineers walked out in August 1974 and joined a small Pennsylvania chipmaker called **MOS Technology**.

questions.prompt: Why did Motorola executives reject Chuck Peddle's 1974 proposal for a 25-dollar microprocessor?
choices: They believed microprocessors were physically incapable of operating below 100 dollars in cost.
They feared an ultra-cheap chip would cannibalize sales of their higher-priced 6800 lineup.
They had already signed an exclusive agreement to manufacture chips only for government defense labs.
They preferred to exit the microprocessor business completely and focus solely on car radios.
questions.explanation: Motorola management worried that selling a 25-dollar microprocessor would undercut and cannibalize profits from its expensive flagship 6800 chip.

questions.prompt: What customer feedback originally convinced Chuck Peddle that a 25-dollar microprocessor was needed?
choices: University laboratories demanded faster scientific calculation speeds regardless of manufacturing price.
Military contractors wanted thicker ceramic chip packages that could withstand extreme heat.
Makers of appliances, terminals, and cash registers wanted microprocessors only at far lower prices.
Large corporate data centers asked for chips capable of driving room-sized magnetic tape drives.
questions.explanation: During customer visits for the 6800, Peddle heard repeatedly from builders of cash registers, terminals, and appliances that microprocessors were compelling but far too pricey.

chunks.title: Two Sibling Chips: Pin Compatibility and an On-Chip Heartbeat
chunks.content_markdown:
At MOS Technology, Peddle and Mensch crafted two closely related sibling chips: the **6501** and the **6502**. To understand why they built both, look at the metal legs—called **pins**—lining each side of a chip's plastic body. Those pins plug into matching holes in a circuit-board socket, carrying electricity, data, and control signals. Two chips have **pin compatibility** when their legs follow the exact same layout, letting engineers swap one processor for another like twisting a standardized lightbulb into an existing lamp socket.

The 6501 offered pin compatibility with Motorola's 6800 so customers could drop it straight into existing boards. The 6502 took a bolder path by adding an **on-chip clock generator**. Every microprocessor relies on a steady electrical pulse—a clock signal—to keep its internal steps marching in rhythm. Motorola's 6800 required a pricey external companion chip just to generate that heartbeat. By building the clock generator right inside the 6502, MOS Technology rearranged several pins while eliminating an entire extra chip from every customer's circuit board.

questions.prompt: What does pin compatibility allow a hardware engineer to do when designing or upgrading a circuit board?
choices: Double the processor's memory capacity without adding any extra storage chips to the board.
Run software written in any human programming language without needing a translator program.
Drop one microprocessor straight into an existing circuit-board socket built for another chip.
Connect a processor directly to a wall outlet without converting household alternating current.
questions.explanation: Pin compatibility means two chips share the exact same pin layout, allowing one to plug directly into a socket originally wired for the other.

questions.prompt: How did the 6502's on-chip clock generator save money compared with Motorola's 6800?
choices: It removed the need for an expensive external companion chip just to supply the timing heartbeat.
It eliminated all circuit-board pins by transmitting every electrical signal over short-range radio.
It allowed the processor to operate completely without electricity during brief pauses in programs.
It allowed a single power wire to carry both electrical current and computer program instructions.
questions.explanation: By generating its timing heartbeat internally, the 6502 spared system builders from buying a separate clock-generator chip like the one Motorola's 6800 required.

chunks.title: Glass Jars in San Francisco: The WESCON Bombshell
chunks.content_markdown:
In September 1975, electronics engineers poured into San Francisco for **WESCON**, the Western Electronic Show and Convention. Ahead of the show, MOS Technology ran full-page magazine advertisements that looked like a misprint: 20 dollars for a 6501, and 25 dollars for a 6502—undercutting leading rivals like the Motorola 6800 and Intel 8080 (both listed near 179 dollars) by nearly an order of magnitude—almost ten times less. Many engineers assumed the ads were a publicity stunt or a typo.

Because WESCON rules prohibited direct cash sales on the exhibition floor, MOS Technology rented a suite at the nearby St. Francis Hotel and invited skeptics to see for themselves. Inside sat large glass jars brimming with real 6501 and 6502 chips, flanked by thick blue programming manuals. Engineers lined up down the corridor, handing over twenty-five dollars in cash and walking out with an honest-to-goodness microprocessor in their pocket. Hobbyists who could never afford a 179-dollar chip suddenly held computing power within reach.

questions.prompt: Why did MOS Technology sell its 6501 and 6502 chips from a San Francisco hotel suite during WESCON 1975?
choices: Motorola had bought out every exhibition booth inside the main San Francisco convention hall.
WESCON convention rules prohibited exhibitors from conducting direct cash sales on the showroom floor.
The chips were too sensitive to indoor fluorescent lights to be displayed in the convention center.
California state law banned selling semiconductor manuals anywhere outside licensed hotel lobbies.
questions.explanation: Convention regulations barred over-the-counter sales on the exhibit floor, so MOS Technology operated a bustling cash-and-carry suite at the St. Francis Hotel nearby.

questions.prompt: Roughly how did MOS Technology's 25-dollar 6502 compare in price with flagship rivals like the 6800 and 8080 in September 1975?
choices: It cost roughly the same as rival chips once buyers included a separate power transformer.
It undercut rival flagship microprocessors by roughly fifteen percent on bulk factory orders.
It sold for roughly double the price of competing chips because of its built-in clock circuit.
It undercut leading rivals priced around 179 dollars by nearly an order of magnitude.
questions.explanation: At 25 dollars (and 20 dollars for the 6501), MOS Technology's chips cost nearly ten times less than flagship rivals selling around 179 dollars.

chunks.title: Motorola's Lawsuit and the Ironic Survival of the 6502
chunks.content_markdown:
Motorola did not sit quietly while its former engineers sold 20-dollar drop-in replacements for its flagship processor. In November 1975, Motorola filed a fierce lawsuit against MOS Technology alleging misuse of trade secrets and targeting the **6501** directly. Because the 6501 boasted pin compatibility with the 6800, any company already building 6800 boards could yank out Motorola's pricey processor and snap in a 20-dollar 6501 overnight.

Facing mounting legal bills, MOS Technology agreed to a settlement in 1976 that paid Motorola damages, arranged patent cross-licensing, and permanently retired the 6501 from the market. Here came the twist: the **6502** stayed completely legal to sell! Because its built-in **on-chip clock generator** had forced Peddle and Mensch to rearrange the pins, the 6502 was not a drop-in 6800 clone. Ironically, killing the 6501 nudged an entire generation of designers away from older 6800 sockets and onto cleaner, cheaper circuit boards built specifically around the 6502.

questions.prompt: Why did the 6502 survive Motorola's lawsuit even though MOS Technology had to retire the 6501?
choices: The 6502 used a different pin layout for its on-chip clock generator rather than copying 6800 sockets.
The 6502 was manufactured outside the United States and therefore sat beyond federal court reach.
Motorola agreed to purchase every 6502 chip from MOS Technology as a backup inventory supply.
The 6502 contained no instructions for addition or subtraction and did not compete with the 6800.
questions.explanation: Unlike the pin-compatible 6501, the 6502 had rearranged pins to support its on-chip clock generator, keeping it distinct from 6800 sockets and free to remain on the market.

questions.prompt: What ironic long-term effect did the forced retirement of the 6501 have on personal-computer hardware?
choices: It forced hobbyists to switch back to 179-dollar Motorola 6800 boards for the rest of the decade.
It steered hardware builders to design fresh, simpler, lower-cost boards around the 6502 instead.
It delayed the arrival of all home computers until Motorola's patents expired in the late 1980s.
It persuaded MOS Technology to abandon microprocessors and focus solely on digital wristwatches.
questions.explanation: With the drop-in 6501 gone, engineers embraced the 6502 directly, taking full advantage of its built-in clock generator to design leaner, cheaper circuit boards.

chunks.title: From Price Shock to the Silicon Puzzle
chunks.content_markdown:
Looking back across those hectic fourteen months between August 1974 and late 1975, every piece of the 6502's origin story clicked together like clockwork. A disagreement over whether computing belonged only to big corporations sent Chuck Peddle, Bill Mensch, and their colleagues out Motorola's door. A bold hotel-suite sales stunt at WESCON shattered the mental barrier that a microprocessor had to cost hundreds of dollars. And a courtroom settlement that buried the pin-compatible 6501 accidentally cleared the runway for the 6502 and its cost-saving **on-chip clock generator**.

Yet one stubborn riddle still baffled semiconductor executives across Silicon Valley. Everyone in the industry knew how expensive it was to manufacture intricate silicon chips—and many insisted MOS Technology must be losing money on every 25-dollar 6502 just to grab headlines. They were wrong. In the next section, we zoom inside that fingernail-sized sliver of silicon to discover how smart circuit design and clever factory craftsmanship made a 25-dollar processor genuinely profitable.

questions.prompt: Which sequence accurately captures the turning points that launched the 6502 into the marketplace?
choices: Motorola lawsuit, 1974 breakaway to MOS Technology, WESCON hotel-suite sales, and 6501 launch.
WESCON hotel-suite sales, 1974 breakaway from Motorola, 6502 retirement, and 6501 survival.
1974 breakaway, 1975 WESCON debut, and lawsuit retiring the 6501 while sparing the 6502.
1975 WESCON debut at Motorola, 1976 spin-off of MOS Technology, and return to external clock chips.
questions.explanation: Peddle's team left Motorola in 1974, stunned WESCON with 20- and 25-dollar chips in September 1975, and then settled Motorola's lawsuit by retiring the 6501 while keeping the 6502.

questions.prompt: What lingering business mystery puzzled rival chip executives immediately after the 6502's 25-dollar debut?
choices: How MOS Technology persuaded WESCON organizers to move the convention to Pennsylvania.
Whether customers would prefer blue reference manuals over red loose-leaf binders.
Why Motorola refused to sell external clock chips to companies located in California.
How MOS Technology could manufacture and sell a working microprocessor profitably for just 25 dollars.
questions.explanation: Given how costly and defect-prone 1970s chip fabrication was, rivals doubted anyone could cover factory costs—let alone turn a profit—at 25 dollars per processor.

sections.title: 2. Silicon Economics: 3,510 Transistors, Depletion-Mode NMOS & Wafer Yield
sections.summary: Demystify how MOS Technology turned a real profit on a 25-dollar processor by pairing a minimalist 3,510-transistor architecture with single-supply depletion-mode NMOS circuits, a compact hand-drawn silicon die, and optical mask-defect repair that dramatically boosted wafer yield.

chunks.title: Why a 25-Dollar Chip Looked Financially Impossible
chunks.content_markdown:
To see why Silicon Valley veterans doubted MOS Technology's 25-dollar price tag, picture how microprocessors are manufactured. Factory workers do not build one chip at a time. Instead, they print dozens of identical circuit patterns across a thin, round, palm-sized disc of ultra-pure crystal called a **silicon wafer**, then slice that disc into individual tiny squares called **dies**. Each working die gets wired into a protective plastic package with metal pins.

Here was the catch in 1975: chip factories were fighting an invisible war against microscopic flaws. A single stray dust mote or tiny crystal defect could short-circuit an entire die, turning it into worthless scrap. When major chipmakers produced large, intricate processors, they routinely threw away seventy to ninety percent of every finished wafer! Paying full factory costs while discarding most of your output forced retail prices sky-high—so selling a profitable microprocessor for 25 dollars meant rewriting the math of chip fabrication.

questions.prompt: In semiconductor manufacturing, how do a silicon wafer and a die relate to each other?
choices: A silicon wafer is the protective plastic shell placed around a fragile metal die.
A silicon wafer is a crystal disc printed with identical circuits and sliced into individual dies.
A die is the glass lens that projects light onto a wafer during the testing phase.
A die is a bundle of ten stacked silicon wafers wired together inside a single socket.
questions.explanation: Factories fabricate many identical processor circuits simultaneously on one round silicon wafer, then cut the wafer into individual rectangular dies.

questions.prompt: Why did rival chipmakers in 1975 have to charge well over 100 dollars for their flagship microprocessors?
choices: Raw sand used to refine silicon crystal cost more per ounce than refined silver.
Each processor had to be assembled under a microscope from hand-soldered vacuum tubes.
Most dies failed from microscopic flaws, forcing the few working chips to cover wafer costs.
Federal trade rules set a mandatory minimum wholesale price on all commercial electronic microprocessors.
questions.explanation: Because 70 to 90 percent of large, complex dies were ruined by microscopic flaws, the handful of surviving chips had to shoulder the entire cost of processing the wafer.

chunks.title: Minimalist Silicon: 3,510 Transistors and Depletion-Mode NMOS
chunks.content_markdown:
MOS Technology's first cost-cutting weapon was ruthless simplicity. Every microprocessor is built out of microscopic electronic switches called **transistors**, which flip on and off to process patterns of zeros and ones. The fewer transistors a design requires, the less silicon space it occupies. Peddle and Mensch pared the 6502 down to just **3,510 transistors**—far leaner than many rival processors—by trimming duplicate internal storage and organizing control logic into clean, regular grids.

Just as important was the switch recipe they chose: **depletion-mode NMOS**. In plain terms, NMOS transistors carry electrical signals using nimble, negatively charged electrons, and the 'depletion-mode' twist added tiny built-in load switches that stayed gently conductive to pull signal wires cleanly high without extra power lines. Older silicon recipes required bulky load transistors or three separate power-supply voltages to switch cleanly. Depletion-mode NMOS ran from a single 5-volt supply, packed switches tighter together, and switched crisply—shrinking the 6502's footprint while making customers' power supplies far simpler too.

questions.prompt: How did trimming the 6502 down to just 3,510 transistors help MOS Technology lower chip cost?
choices: It allowed the factory to skip slicing silicon wafers and sell whole discs instead.
It reduced the chip's physical silicon area, shrinking each die and lowering defect exposure.
It eliminated the need for metal pins by storing electrical power inside a tiny battery.
It let technicians assemble each processor manually using ordinary copper telegraph wire.
questions.explanation: Using only 3,510 transistors let the 6502 occupy a much smaller patch of silicon, fitting more dies on every wafer and exposing each die to fewer random defects.

questions.prompt: What practical engineering advantages did depletion-mode NMOS bring to the 6502?
choices: It allowed the chip to run on three separate high-voltage rails for extra brightness.
It replaced silicon wafers with flexible plastic strips that resisted accidental cracking.
It enabled faster, tighter-packed switches operating cleanly from a single 5-volt power supply.
It stored permanent user software inside the transistors even when power was turned off.
questions.explanation: Depletion-mode NMOS used compact, naturally conductive pull-up transistors to pack circuits tightly, switch quickly, and run cleanly from a single 5-volt supply.

chunks.title: Hand-Drawn Dies and the Patio-Tile Math of Wafer Yield
chunks.content_markdown:
To see why die size makes or breaks chip economics, let us define **wafer yield**: the percentage of dies on a finished silicon wafer that pass testing and actually work. Imagine scattering ten random pebbles onto a square tiled patio, where any pebble cracks the tile it lands on. If the patio uses twenty giant tiles, nearly half your tiles shatter. Now shrink the tiles to one-quarter their area so eighty tiles fit on the exact same patio. Those same ten pebbles now ruin far fewer tiles as a share of the whole—leaving roughly seventy intact tiles instead of ten!

Bill Mensch and MOS Technology's layout artists turned that math into an art form. Working without modern automated layout software, they hand-drew the 6502's circuit layers onto giant translucent sheets, tucking wires together until the entire 3,510-transistor die measured roughly four millimeters across. Shrinking the die delivered a double windfall: far more dies squeezed onto each wafer, and a much higher fraction dodged random dust.

questions.prompt: What does wafer yield measure in a semiconductor fabrication plant?
choices: The percentage of dies on a finished silicon wafer that pass testing and work properly.
The total number of hours a finished microprocessor runs before its switches wear out.
The maximum clock speed a processor reaches after being mounted in a plastic socket.
The weight of pure quartz sand needed to melt and grow a single silicon crystal cylinder.
questions.explanation: Wafer yield is the fraction or percentage of individual dies cut from a processed silicon wafer that test as fully functional chips.

questions.prompt: According to the tiled-patio analogy, why does shrinking a processor's die deliver a double economic payoff?
choices: Smaller dies require cheaper sand and can skip all electrical testing before shipment.
Smaller dies draw zero electrical current and eliminate the need for protective plastic cases.
Smaller dies pack more chips onto each wafer while also losing a smaller share to random defects.
Smaller dies automatically repair cracked silicon crystals when heated inside a factory oven.
questions.explanation: Just like shrinking patio tiles against ten scattered pebbles, a smaller die fits more candidate chips on every wafer and increases the share that dodge random flaws.

chunks.title: The Hidden Secret Weapon: Optical Mask-Defect Repair
chunks.content_markdown:
Shrinking the die solved random dust, yet an even sneakier yield killer lurked in 1970s chip plants: the **photomask**. Chipmakers print circuits onto silicon wafers by shining bright ultraviolet light through a patterned glass master stencil—the photomask—much like making photographic prints from a film negative. Random dust ruins only one die on one wafer, whereas a tiny dark speck or pinhole on a photomask stamps the exact same fatal flaw onto every single wafer printed from it!

MOS Technology beat that problem with painstaking **optical mask-defect repair**. Before exposing expensive silicon wafers, technicians inspected each glass photomask under high-powered microscopes, using focused optical tools to zap away stray dark specks and patch missing clear spots. Combined with the compact hand-drawn die, clean masks lifted 6502 **wafer yield** from the industry norm of roughly ten to thirty percent up toward an astonishing seventy percent. That factory discipline turned 25-dollar chips from a reckless gamble into a cash cow.

questions.prompt: Why is a microscopic flaw on a glass photomask far more damaging to wafer yield than a speck of dust on one silicon wafer?
choices: A photomask flaw stamps the exact same circuit defect repeatedly onto every wafer printed from it.
A photomask flaw melts the factory's ultraviolet lamp and halts production for several weeks.
A photomask flaw slows down the finished chip's clock generator by half on every working die.
A photomask flaw dissolves the metal pins after the chip is soldered onto a customer's board.
questions.explanation: Because a photomask acts like a master stencil reused across many wafers, a defect on the mask reproduces the same broken circuit again and again instead of ruining just one die.

questions.prompt: How did optical mask-defect repair help MOS Technology push 6502 wafer yields dramatically above typical 1975 industry levels?
choices: Technicians used optical scanners to boost each chip's transistor count after the wafer was sliced.
Technicians switched from glass masks to flexible plastic films that required zero optical inspection.
Technicians painted reflective silver over finished dies so broken wires would reconnect automatically.
Technicians inspected glass photomasks microscopically to remove stray spots and patch flaws before printing.
questions.explanation: By inspecting photomasks under microscopes and optically fixing specks and pinholes before wafer exposure, MOS Technology eliminated repeating defects and drove wafer yield dramatically higher.

chunks.title: Lean Silicon Meets an Unexpected Speed Surprise
chunks.content_markdown:
Now the 25-dollar riddle dissolves into clean engineering arithmetic. MOS Technology did not lose money on the 6502; it redesigned the entire economics of silicon from top to bottom. Trimming the logic to **3,510 transistors**, adopting compact single-supply **depletion-mode NMOS**, hand-drawing a tiny die, and pioneering **optical mask-defect repair** pushed **wafer yield** high enough that each surviving 6502 cost only a few dollars to fabricate.

Normally, cutting a product's price and parts count so drastically leaves you with a sluggish bargain-bin compromise. Yet engineers who plugged a 6502 into test benches got a second shock as big as the price tag: even ticking along at a leisurely one million beats per second, the 6502 kept pace with—and often outran—famous rival chips ticking two to four times faster! In the next section, we unpack how a clever twist in byte ordering and overlapped timing turned bare-bones silicon into remarkable speed.

questions.prompt: Which combination of engineering practices made MOS Technology's 25-dollar 6502 genuinely profitable?
choices: Triple-voltage circuits, oversized automated dies, external clock chips, and low-volume boutique sales.
3,510 minimalist transistors, depletion-mode NMOS, a compact hand-drawn die, and optical mask-defect repair.
Larger dies, older multi-voltage switches, twenty-percent wafer yields, and high-margin industrial pricing.
Pin compatibility with the 6800, thick ceramic packaging, and outsourcing fabrication to Motorola.
questions.explanation: Minimalist transistor count, single-supply depletion-mode NMOS, a tight hand-drawn die, and optical mask-defect repair combined to push wafer yield high and unit cost low.

questions.prompt: What surprising real-world performance result greeted engineers who benchmarked the inexpensive 6502 against pricier rivals?
choices: It required ten times more clock beats than rival chips just to add two small numbers.
It only matched competing processors when cooled inside liquid-nitrogen laboratory baths.
It needed twice as many external support chips to reach half the speed of older designs.
It matched or outran rival microprocessors that ticked two to four times faster on paper.
questions.explanation: Despite its stripped-down 3,510-transistor design and modest clock speed, the 6502's efficient internal timing let it rival competitors running at two to four times the clock rate.

sections.title: 3. Little-Endian Byte Order & the 2-Stage Fetch/Execute Overlap
sections.summary: Uncover how a 1 MHz 6502 rivaled higher-clocked competitors by introducing little-endian byte order—contrasted directly with the 6800's big-endian layout—and the 6502's 2-stage fetch/execute overlap, which let the chip add an index offset to the low address byte while simultaneously reading the high byte across 256-byte memory pages.

chunks.title: The One-Megahertz Speed Paradox
chunks.content_markdown:
Every microprocessor marches to an electronic metronome, and engineers measure that tempo in **megahertz (MHz)**—millions of ticks, or **clock cycles**, per second. Most early 6502 computers ran at a calm $$1\text{ MHz}$$, meaning one million ticks per second. Meanwhile, famous rival processors of the late 1970s proudly advertised $$2\text{ MHz}$$ or even $$4\text{ MHz}$$ clock speeds. On a glossy magazine spec sheet, the 6502 looked two to four times slower.

Yet when programmers ran real games, spreadsheets, and text editors side by side, that $$1\text{ MHz}$$ 6502 routinely matched or beat its faster-ticking rivals. How? Imagine two painters racing to paint a fence: Painter A waves a tiny brush four times per second, while Painter B sweeps a wide roller once per second. Raw tempo means little until you ask how much real work happens on each beat. Rival chips burned four or more clock cycles just to read one byte from memory, whereas the 6502 accomplished useful memory work on nearly every single tick.

questions.prompt: What does a processor clock speed of 1 megahertz (1 MHz) measure?
choices: One million electronic metronome ticks, or clock cycles, occurring every second.
One million separate transistors flipping inside the silicon die at the exact same instant.
One million bytes of permanent program storage built inside the plastic chip housing.
One million complete computer programs finished and saved to tape during a single minute.
questions.explanation: One megahertz equals one million clock cycles per second, setting the steady timing rhythm that paces a processor's internal steps.

questions.prompt: Why could a 1 MHz 6502 match or outperform rival processors advertised at 2 MHz or 4 MHz?
choices: Its on-chip clock generator secretly ran four times faster than printed on its datasheet.
It accomplished useful memory and calculation work in far fewer clock cycles per instruction.
It skipped reading instructions from memory and guessed what programs wanted to do next.
It only allowed simple addition programs while banning slower multiplication or text handling.
questions.explanation: Raw clock rate only counts ticks per second; because the 6502 needed far fewer ticks per instruction than its rivals, a 1 MHz 6502 delivered comparable or faster real work.

chunks.title: Pages, Bytes, and Flipping Motorola's Order Upside Down
chunks.content_markdown:
To see the 6502's speed secret, we need three quick building blocks. Computers store information in tiny on/off switches called **bits**, bundled in groups of eight called **bytes**. One byte holds $$2^8 = 256$$ possible values, written in base-16 **hexadecimal** shorthand using digits `0`–`9` and letters `A`–`F` (10 through 15) with a `0x` prefix, so two digits span `0x00` (0) to `0xFF` (255). To reach $$2^{16} = 65{,}536$$ memory slots, the 6502 pairs two bytes into a 16-bit address: a **high byte** naming a 256-byte **memory page** (like a hotel floor), and a **low byte** picking one of 256 rooms on that floor.

When storing a 16-bit address like `0x1234` across two memory slots, Motorola's 6800 stored the high byte `0x12` first and `0x34` second—a human-friendly style called **big-endian** order. The 6502 flipped that convention completely into **little-endian byte order**, storing the **low byte** (`0x34`) first at the lower address and the **high byte** (`0x12`) second! That backwards-looking layout was no quirk—it unlocked a remarkable timing trick.

questions.prompt: In a 16-bit memory address on the 6502, what role does the high byte play compared with the low byte?
choices: The high byte selects a 256-byte memory page, while the low byte picks a slot inside it.
The high byte stores the letter name of a file, while the low byte stores the text inside that file.
The high byte sets the processor's megahertz speed, while the low byte controls the power voltage.
The high byte holds only odd-numbered addresses, while the low byte holds only even-numbered addresses.
questions.explanation: Like a hotel floor and room number, the high byte identifies which 256-byte memory page is targeted, and the low byte picks one of the 256 bytes on that page.

questions.prompt: How is the 16-bit address 0x408A stored across two consecutive memory bytes under the 6502's little-endian byte order?
choices: The high byte 0x40 is stored first, followed immediately by the low byte 0x8A.
Both bytes are added together and stored as a single compressed byte 0xCA.
The low byte 0x8A is stored first, followed immediately by the high byte 0x40.
The digits are reversed completely so 0xA8 is stored first and 0x04 is stored second.
questions.explanation: Little-endian byte order keeps the bits inside each byte intact but places the least significant (low) byte first (0x8A) and the most significant (high) byte second (0x40).

chunks.title: Doing Two Things at Once: 2-Stage Fetch/Execute Overlap
chunks.content_markdown:
Why put the low byte first? Because the 6502 uses **fetch/execute overlap**—a lean two-stage assembly line where fetching the next byte from memory happens at the very same moment the processor finishes working on the byte it just read. Picture a busy barista who steams milk for drink number one while simultaneously reaching for the cup for drink number two; neither hand sits idle.

Watch this magic unfold when the 6502 adds an offset of `5` to a base address `0x1230` to look up a table entry. On Tick 1, it fetches the instruction code. On Tick 2, thanks to **little-endian byte order**, it fetches the **low byte** `0x30` first. On Tick 3, two jobs run in parallel: while memory hands over the **high byte** `0x12`, the 6502's 8-bit adder computes `0x30 + 5 = 0x35`! On Tick 4, the finished address `0x1235` is already ready to read. Had the high byte arrived first, the adder would have waited around uselessly for an extra cycle.

questions.prompt: Why did fetching the low address byte before the high byte make indexed lookups faster on the 6502?
choices: It let the processor ignore the high byte completely whenever a program ran above 1 MHz.
It shrank every 16-bit address down to 4 bits so all data fit on a single pin.
It prevented the memory chips from needing any electrical power during the first two ticks.
It allowed the chip to add an offset to the low byte while simultaneously fetching the high byte.
questions.explanation: Receiving the low byte first meant the 6502's adder could immediately add the offset to it during the very same clock cycle that memory supplied the high byte.

questions.prompt: What core idea does the 6502's 2-stage fetch/execute overlap introduce?
choices: Running two completely unrelated user programs on two separate silicon dies in one socket.
Storing every instruction twice in memory so a backup copy is ready if one byte fails.
Overlapping the execution or math step of one byte with fetching the next byte from memory.
Pausing the memory bus completely until an entire multi-step calculation finishes every operation.
questions.explanation: Fetch/execute overlap is a simple two-stage pipeline that keeps both the memory bus and internal execution logic busy simultaneously instead of waiting in turns.

chunks.title: Crossing a Page Boundary: The Clever One-Tick Carry Tax
chunks.content_markdown:
Wait—what happens when adding an offset to the low byte spills past `0xFF` (255)? Suppose our base address is `0x12F8` and our offset is `0x10`. During Tick 3, while memory delivers the high byte `0x12`, the 6502's built-in 8-bit adding circuit computes `0xF8 + 0x10` (248 plus 16 equals 264) and gets `0x08`—with a **carry** of `1`! That carry means our destination has stepped across a **memory page** boundary from page `0x12` up into page `0x13` (true address `0x1308`).

Because the minimalist 6502 owns only a single 8-bit adder, it cannot add that carry to the high byte until Tick 4. So on Tick 4 it makes a quick fix-up tick—reading a throwaway byte at `0x1208` while bumping `0x12` up to `0x13`—and then reads the real byte from `0x1308` on Tick 5. Instead of wasting hundreds of transistors on a bulky 16-bit adder, Peddle and Mensch made a shrewd engineering bet: keep same-page accesses blazingly fast, and pay one extra tick only when a carry crosses a page line.

questions.prompt: When does an indexed memory read on the 6502 incur one extra clock cycle to fix up its address?
choices: Whenever the processor switches from reading numbers to reading text characters.
Whenever adding the offset to the low byte produces a carry that crosses into the next memory page.
Whenever the offset equals zero and the processor must verify that the low byte did not change.
Whenever the high byte of the address is an even hexadecimal number such as 0x12 or 0x24.
questions.explanation: If adding the offset to the low byte overflows past 0xFF, the 8-bit adder needs one extra cycle to add the carry of 1 to the high byte before reading from the next page.

questions.prompt: Which of these indexed address calculations crosses a 256-byte memory page boundary and costs an extra clock cycle?
choices: Base address 0x2010 plus an offset of 0x05.
Base address 0x2080 plus an offset of 0x20.
Base address 0x2000 plus an offset of 0xFF.
Base address 0x20F0 plus an offset of 0x20.
questions.explanation: Adding 0x20 to 0xF0 overflows 0xFF (producing 0x10 with a carry of 1), moving from page 0x20 to page 0x21 (0x2110), whereas the other three stay within page 0x20.

chunks.title: Speed Without Waste—And a Surprising Scarcity Ahead
chunks.content_markdown:
Everything about the 6502's unexpected speed now snaps into focus. Choosing **little-endian byte order** over Motorola's big-endian layout was not stubbornness—it fed the low address byte into the processor first so **fetch/execute overlap** could compute indexed offsets in the shadow of reading the high byte. Paired with a lean 8-bit adder that only charged a one-cycle toll across **memory page** boundaries, most common 6502 instructions wrapped up in just two to four clock ticks, letting a $$1\text{ MHz}$$ chip stand shoulder to shoulder with $$2\text{ MHz}$$ and $$4\text{ MHz}$$ rivals.

Yet staying slim at 3,510 transistors demanded one huge sacrifice inside the chip itself: there was barely any silicon left for built-in scratchpad slots to hold working numbers! Programmers arriving from larger processors opened the 6502 manual and blinked at how few internal slots it offered. In the next section, we meet that minimalist internal layout—and see how the 6502 turned the very first page of external memory into a turbo-charged substitute.

questions.prompt: How did little-endian byte order and fetch/execute overlap work together inside the 6502?
choices: Little-endian order doubled the number of pins so fetch/execute overlap could read two pages simultaneously.
Little-endian order delivered the low byte first so the adder could compute offsets while memory fetched the high byte.
Fetch/execute overlap converted every little-endian program into big-endian Motorola code before running it.
Fetch/execute overlap disabled the clock generator whenever two bytes arrived from the same memory page.
questions.explanation: Placing the low address byte first let the 6502 overlap low-byte address math with fetching the high byte, squeezing maximum useful work out of every clock cycle.

questions.prompt: Why did the 6502's 3,510-transistor budget force an unusual design choice for its internal working storage?
choices: It left room for sixteen giant 32-bit workbenches that took ten cycles each to empty.
It forced the chip to store every working number permanently on external magnetic cassette tape.
It left very little silicon space for built-in scratchpad slots, requiring a clever memory shortcut.
It prevented the chip from keeping track of which instruction it was currently executing.
questions.explanation: Keeping the die tiny left minimal room for on-chip registers, pushing MOS Technology to lean heavily on fast access to the very first page of external memory.

sections.title: 4. The Lean Register Model & Zero Page Pseudo-Registers
sections.summary: Unpack the 6502's deliberately sparse internal registers—a single 8-bit accumulator (A), two 8-bit index registers (X and Y), and an 8-bit stack pointer—and explore how shorter, faster instructions turned the first 256 bytes of RAM, Zero Page (0x0000–0x00FF), into a high-speed bank of pseudo-registers.

chunks.title: A Surprisingly Bare Workbench Inside the Chip
chunks.content_markdown:
Inside any microprocessor sit tiny, ultra-fast storage cubbies called **registers**. Think of registers as the ingredients held right in a chef's hands, whereas main computer memory is the walk-in pantry across the kitchen. Rival 1970s chips boasted generous on-chip cubbies: Intel's 8080 offered seven general-purpose 8-bit registers, and Motorola's 6800 provided two math accumulators alongside full 16-bit index and stack registers.

Programmers opening the 6502 manual for the first time stared in disbelief at how sparse its silicon workbench looked. To stay lean at 3,510 transistors, Peddle and Mensch gave the 6502 just one 8-bit **accumulator** (`A`, the main slot for arithmetic), two 8-bit **index registers** (`X` and `Y`, handy for counting and stepping through lists), and a single 8-bit **stack pointer** (`S`, tracking a temporary bookmark pile), plus a 16-bit program counter tracking the next instruction and an 8-bit status register recording test results. How could serious software thrive with barely four working cubbies?

questions.prompt: Why did MOS Technology give the 6502 far fewer internal registers than rival chips such as the Intel 8080 or Motorola 6800?
choices: Adding extra on-chip registers consumed substantial silicon area and would have bloated the tiny 3,510-transistor die.
Depletion-mode NMOS switches could electrically support no more than four bytes of storage inside one package.
Early programmers requested fewer registers because they struggled to remember more than three alphabetical names.
Motorola's 1975 lawsuit prohibited MOS Technology from placing a second accumulator inside any processor.
questions.explanation: On-chip registers require many transistors and wiring routes; stripping the register bank to the bone kept the 6502 die tiny, high-yield, and inexpensive.

questions.prompt: Which set accurately describes the 6502's lean core working registers?
choices: Two 16-bit accumulators, one 16-bit index register, and a 16-bit stack pointer.
Seven interchangeable 8-bit registers paired with a 32-bit scientific-math workbench.
One 8-bit accumulator, two 8-bit index registers, and one 8-bit stack pointer.
Four 8-bit accumulators with no index registers and no built-in stack pointer.
questions.explanation: The 6502's lean programmer model features a single 8-bit accumulator (A), two 8-bit index registers (X and Y), and an 8-bit stack pointer (S), alongside its program counter and status flags.

chunks.title: Zero Page: Turning 256 Bytes of RAM into Pseudo-Registers
chunks.content_markdown:
The answer lay in the very first 256-byte **memory page** of external **RAM** (the computer's erasable working memory): addresses `0x0000` through `0x00FF`, known as **Zero Page**. Instead of paying silicon real estate to build dozens of registers inside the microprocessor die, the 6502 gave Zero Page special VIP treatment so those 256 memory slots acted as a bank of fast **pseudo-registers**—memory locations outside the chip that behave almost like extra built-in registers.

Picture a carpenter's workspace. On-chip registers (`A`, `X`, and `Y`) are the hammer and pencil right in your hands, ordinary RAM is the supply truck parked outside, and **Zero Page** is a wide tool belt around your waist holding 256 quick-draw pockets! Why is Zero Page faster than regular memory? Because every address from `0x0000` to `0x00FF` starts with the exact same high byte (`0x00`). Special 6502 instructions skip storing and fetching that zero high byte altogether.

questions.prompt: Which memory addresses make up the 6502's Zero Page?
choices: The final 256 bytes at the top of memory from 0xFF00 through 0xFFFF.
The first 256 bytes of memory from 0x0000 through 0x00FF.
The second 256 bytes of memory from 0x0100 through 0x01FF.
Every address whose low byte ends in zero across all 65,536 memory locations.
questions.explanation: Zero Page is memory page zero—the 256 bytes spanning addresses 0x0000 through 0x00FF, all of which share the high byte 0x00.

questions.prompt: How did Zero Page pseudo-registers compensate for the 6502's sparse on-chip register set?
choices: They added an extra external clock generator that tripled the speed of accumulator math.
They permanently stored read-only copies of user software inside the processor's metal pins.
They gave programmers 256 quick-access memory slots reachable with shorter, faster instructions.
They automatically copied every variable onto cassette tape whenever accumulator A filled up.
questions.explanation: By letting instructions omit the 0x00 high byte, Zero Page turned the first 256 bytes of RAM into compact, fast-access pseudo-registers right at the programmer's fingertips.

chunks.title: Saving Bytes and Clock Ticks: Ordinary RAM vs. Zero Page
chunks.content_markdown:
Let us trace a concrete example to feel the difference **Zero Page** makes in real code. Suppose a video game wants to load the player's current score into accumulator `A`. First, imagine storing that score in ordinary RAM at address `0x2045` (on memory page `0x20`). To fetch it, the instruction takes **three bytes** of program code—the operation code (or **opcode**, telling the chip what action to perform), the low byte `0x45`, and the high byte `0x20`—and burns **four clock cycles**: fetch opcode, fetch `0x45`, fetch `0x20`, and finally read the score.

Now move that score into **Zero Page** at `0x0045` (written simply as `0x45`). The instruction shrinks to just **two bytes**—opcode plus `0x45`—and completes in **three clock cycles**! While reading `0x45`, the 6502 simply supplies `0x00` as the high byte for free. That single design choice cuts instruction size by a third and execution time by a quarter every time a program touches its hottest variables.

questions.prompt: How does loading a value from Zero Page address 0x0045 compare with loading from ordinary memory address 0x2045 on the 6502?
choices: The Zero Page load uses 4 bytes and 5 clock cycles because the chip must unlock special RAM protection.
Both loads use the exact same 3 bytes and 4 cycles, differing only in how programmers name them.
The Zero Page load takes 1 clock cycle because Zero Page physically resides inside the 6502 silicon die.
The Zero Page load uses 2 bytes and 3 clock cycles, compared with 3 bytes and 4 clock cycles for 0x2045.
questions.explanation: Skipping the 0x00 high byte trims a Zero Page load from 3 bytes and 4 clock cycles down to 2 bytes and 3 clock cycles.

questions.prompt: Why can the 6502 omit the high address byte inside a Zero Page instruction?
choices: The chip guesses the high byte by copying whatever number currently sits in accumulator A.
Every Zero Page address shares the high byte 0x00, so the hardware automatically supplies 0x00 internally.
Zero Page instructions only operate on numbers smaller than 16 and ignore all upper memory wires.
The computer's keyboard controller transmits the missing high byte during every second clock tick.
questions.explanation: Because Zero Page specifically means page 0x00 (0x0000–0x00FF), the 6502 knows the high byte is always 0x00 without reading it from memory.

chunks.title: The Real-Estate Scramble for 256 Precious Bytes
chunks.content_markdown:
Motorola's 6800 actually planted the seed for this idea with its own 'direct addressing' mode on the first 256 bytes of RAM. Yet MOS Technology elevated **Zero Page** from a minor convenience into the beating heart of the entire 6502 architecture—adding rich indexed operations and special addressing shortcuts that worked *only* on Zero Page.

That superpower created an amusing twist across early personal computers: those 256 bytes became the most fiercely contested beachfront property in computing! On machines like the Apple II or Commodore home computers, the operating system, the built-in programming language, disk routines, and user programs all hungered for **Zero Page** **pseudo-registers**. Reference manuals published elaborate street maps showing exactly which Zero Page bytes belonged to the system and which handful stayed safe for hobbyists. Losing track of a single shared Zero Page byte—and letting two routines scribble over the same pocket—caused some of the trickiest crashes in 1970s software!

questions.prompt: How did the 6502's Zero Page relate to Motorola's earlier 6800 microprocessor?
choices: The 6800 lacked external RAM completely, so MOS Technology invented memory pages from scratch.
The 6502 expanded on the 6800's direct-page concept by making Zero Page central with exclusive addressing powers.
The 6502 shrank the 6800's 4,096-byte direct page down to 256 bytes to save external pins.
The 6800 and 6502 both banned operating systems from ever touching addresses 0x0000 through 0x00FF.
questions.explanation: While Motorola's 6800 offered direct addressing on the first 256 bytes, the 6502 made Zero Page the centerpiece of its architecture with fast pseudo-registers and exclusive addressing modes.

questions.prompt: Why did Zero Page bytes become fiercely contested real estate on real 6502 home computers?
choices: Zero Page was the only portion of memory able to remember data after the computer was unplugged.
Each Zero Page byte cost ten times more to buy at electronics stores than ordinary RAM chips.
Only 256 fast bytes existed, so systems, languages, and user programs all competed for them.
Programs stored outside Zero Page could not execute arithmetic instructions using accumulator A.
questions.explanation: Because Zero Page offered only 256 bytes yet delivered shorter code, faster access, and unique addressing modes, system software and applications constantly competed for free slots.

chunks.title: A Small Die, a Wide Tool Belt—and an 8-Bit Puzzle
chunks.content_markdown:
Look how cleverly the 6502 turned weakness into strength. Instead of spending hundreds of silicon transistors on a bulky internal register file, it offered a crisp minimal set—accumulator `A`, index registers `X` and `Y`, and 8-bit stack pointer `S`—and turned external **Zero Page** (`0x0000`–`0x00FF`) into 256 rapid **pseudo-registers** accessed via compact two-byte instructions. Far from feeling crippled, experienced 6502 coders often found 256 fast tool-belt pockets even handier than seven cramped on-chip slots!

Still, a sharp reader might spot one glaring limitation. Both index registers `X` and `Y` are only **8 bits** wide, meaning each can count only from `0` to `255`—a single memory page! How on earth could a 6502 program step dynamically across a huge document, spreadsheet, or game map spanning tens of thousands of bytes across all 65,536 memory locations? In the next section, we discover how storing full 16-bit addresses right inside Zero Page unlocked two of the most famous addressing tricks in computing history.

questions.prompt: What core architectural trade-off did MOS Technology strike between on-chip registers and Zero Page?
choices: It kept silicon small with sparse on-chip registers while using Zero Page RAM as fast pseudo-registers.
It eliminated all on-chip registers completely and moved the accumulator and program counter into external RAM.
It doubled the transistor count to build 256 Zero Page registers physically inside the 6502 plastic package.
It sacrificed all memory beyond 256 bytes so every instruction could fit inside a single byte.
questions.explanation: By keeping on-chip registers sparse and giving Zero Page fast two-byte access, MOS Technology achieved tiny, profitable silicon without starving programmers of quick working storage.

questions.prompt: What practical addressing puzzle arises directly from the fact that the 6502's X and Y index registers are only 8 bits wide?
choices: Neither X nor Y can ever store an odd number without overflowing accumulator A.
X and Y cannot be incremented by one without restarting the entire computer program.
X and Y only work when the processor's clock generator is slowed below half a megahertz.
Neither X nor Y can hold a full 16-bit address to roam across 65,536 memory slots.
questions.explanation: An 8-bit register holds only values from 0 to 255, so neither X nor Y can hold a full 16-bit address by itself—motivating the 6502's Zero Page indirect addressing modes.

sections.title: 5. Two Signature Indirect Modes: (zp,X) vs. (zp),Y
sections.summary: Master the 6502's two iconic Zero Page indirect addressing modes through intuitive everyday analogies: indexed indirect (zp,X) ('add first, then follow the pointer') for selecting an entry from a table of pointers, versus indirect indexed (zp),Y ('follow the pointer first, then add') for walking swiftly across arrays, text buffers, and screen rows.

chunks.title: Sticky Notes in Zero Page: Meet the 16-Bit Pointer
chunks.content_markdown:
Remember our puzzle from the last section: `X` and `Y` are only 8 bits wide (0 to 255), yet a 6502 computer can hold up to $$65{,}536$$ bytes (64 kilobytes) of memory! If a program wants to edit a long letter, scroll a game screen, or recalculate a budget table whose location changes while the program runs, hardcoding a fixed address inside the instruction will not work—and neither `X` nor `Y` is wide enough to hold a full 16-bit address.

The 6502 solves this elegantly using a **pointer**: a full 16-bit memory address saved across two consecutive bytes in RAM (stored low byte first, in **little-endian byte order**) that 'points' the processor to another location anywhere in memory. Think of a pointer tucked into **Zero Page** as a sticky note in your tool belt with a street address scribbled on it. Because your program can rewrite that sticky note on the fly, the 6502 can reach anywhere across all 64 kilobytes—and combine that pointer with `X` or `Y` in two clever ways.

questions.prompt: What is a pointer in 6502 memory, and how is it stored inside Zero Page?
choices: A single 4-bit flag stored in accumulator A that turns the video screen on or off.
A full 16-bit memory address saved across two consecutive Zero Page bytes in little-endian order.
A physical plastic arrow printed on the motherboard indicating pin number one on the socket.
An 8-bit counter kept inside register X that can only point inside the first 256 bytes.
questions.explanation: On the 6502, a pointer is a 16-bit target address stored across two adjacent bytes (low byte first, high byte second) in memory, especially in Zero Page.

questions.prompt: Why do pointers stored in Zero Page solve the limitation of having only 8-bit index registers X and Y?
choices: Putting a pointer in Zero Page automatically expands registers X and Y from 8 bits to 16 bits.
Zero Page pointers compress an entire 64-kilobyte program into fewer than 256 bytes of RAM.
Storing a pointer in Zero Page eliminates the need for the 6502 to use little-endian byte order.
Two Zero Page bytes hold a changeable 16-bit address reaching any of the 65,536 memory slots.
questions.explanation: A pair of Zero Page bytes acts like a 16-bit address register that software can update dynamically to point anywhere across the entire 64 KB address space.

chunks.title: Add First vs. Follow First: (zp,X) and (zp),Y
chunks.content_markdown:
The 6502 builds two iconic indirect **addressing modes**—rules for telling an instruction where to find its data—around Zero Page pointers, and their parentheses tell the whole story! In **indexed indirect addressing**, written `(zp,X)`, notice that `X` sits **inside** the parentheses: **add `X` first, then follow the pointer**. Picture a filing drawer in Zero Page holding a **table of pointers**—numbered folders where each folder stores a 2-byte address bookmark pointing to a different sound channel or open file. Adding `X` to the starting Zero Page slot `zp` selects *which folder* to open, and the 6502 jumps straight to the address inside.

In **indirect indexed addressing**, written `(zp),Y`, notice that `Y` sits **outside** the parentheses: **follow the pointer first, then add `Y`**. Picture grabbing *one* bookmark from Zero Page that tells you where a chapter begins, flipping straight to that starting address anywhere in memory, and then stepping `Y` slots forward! That single twist—adding after following instead of before—makes `(zp),Y` effortless for walking across ordered lists (arrays), sentences, and screen rows.

questions.prompt: How does the order of operations differ between indexed indirect (zp,X) and indirect indexed (zp),Y?
choices: Both modes follow the pointer first, except (zp,X) subtracts X while (zp),Y adds Y.
(zp,X) reads a single 8-bit address from X, whereas (zp),Y ignores Zero Page completely.
(zp,X) adds X before reading the pointer, while (zp),Y reads the pointer before adding Y.
(zp,X) adds X to the high byte only, whereas (zp),Y adds Y to the low byte only.
questions.explanation: The parentheses mirror the order of work: (zp,X) adds X inside Zero Page first to pick a pointer, while (zp),Y follows the pointer at zp first and adds Y to the resulting 16-bit address.

questions.prompt: Which everyday programming task best matches indexed indirect (zp,X) versus indirect indexed (zp),Y?
choices: Use (zp,X) to pick from a pointer table, and (zp),Y to walk across arrays or screen rows.
Use (zp,X) for walking through a 200-byte text message, and (zp),Y for resetting the clock generator.
Use (zp,X) for multiplying two 16-bit numbers, and (zp),Y for changing the chip's pin layout.
Use (zp,X) exclusively for video screens, and (zp),Y exclusively for reading keyboard power switches.
questions.explanation: (zp,X) shines when selecting among several pointers stored in a Zero Page table, while (zp),Y excels at stepping sequentially across arrays, strings, or rows of screen memory.

chunks.title: Tracing the Exact Bytes: A Side-by-Side Walkthrough
chunks.content_markdown:
Let us trace real numbers so `(zp,X)` and `(zp),Y` feel crystal clear. Suppose our Zero Page holds two 2-byte little-endian pointers side by side:

At `0x0040`–`0x0041`, we store `0x00` then `0x30` (the 16-bit pointer `0x3000`). Right next door, at `0x0042`–`0x0043`, we store `0x10` then `0x50` (the 16-bit pointer `0x5010`).

First, run **indexed indirect** `(0x40,X)` with `X = 2`. Because `X` is inside the parentheses, the 6502 adds `0x40 + 2 = 0x42` *first*. Then it reads the 2-byte pointer sitting at `0x0042`–`0x0043` (`0x5010`) and fetches the byte at **`0x5010`**. Register `X` chose the second bookmark in our table!

Now run **indirect indexed** `(0x40),Y` with `Y = 5`. Because `Y` is outside the parentheses, the 6502 reads the 2-byte pointer at `0x0040`–`0x0041` *first* (`0x3000`), and *then* adds `Y` to that full 16-bit address (`0x3000 + 5`) to fetch the byte at **`0x3005`**. Register `Y` stepped five slots along the array starting at `0x3000`!

questions.prompt: Zero Page holds 0x00, 0x30 at 0x0040–0x0041 and 0x10, 0x50 at 0x0042–0x0043. What final address does indexed indirect (0x40,X) access when X = 2?
choices: 0x3002, because it reads the pointer at 0x0040 and adds 2 to 0x3000.
0x5012, because it adds 2 both to the Zero Page slot and to the final pointer.
0x1050, because pointers in Zero Page are stored in big-endian order.
0x5010, because adding X to 0x40 reaches 0x0042 and reads its little-endian pointer.
questions.explanation: Indexed indirect (0x40,X) adds X = 2 to 0x40 first (reaching 0x0042), then reads the little-endian bytes 0x10 (low) and 0x50 (high) to access 0x5010.

questions.prompt: Using the same Zero Page memory (0x00, 0x30 at 0x0040–0x0041), what final address does indirect indexed (0x40),Y access when Y = 5?
choices: 0x3005, because it reads the little-endian pointer 0x3000 from 0x0040–0x0041 and then adds Y = 5.
0x0045, because it adds Y = 5 to 0x0040 and reads directly from Zero Page without following a pointer.
0x5015, because adding Y automatically skips over the first pointer to the second entry.
0x0530, because it adds Y = 5 to the high byte of the pointer instead of the low byte.
questions.explanation: Indirect indexed (0x40),Y first reads the 16-bit little-endian pointer at 0x0040–0x0041 (0x3000), then adds Y = 5 to reach 0x3005.

chunks.title: Why (zp),Y Ruled Everyday Code—And a Subtle Wraparound Twist
chunks.content_markdown:
On a reference chart, `(zp,X)` and `(zp),Y` look like equal twins. In real 6502 programs, however, **indirect indexed `(zp),Y`** was the undisputed workhorse, appearing dramatically more often than `(zp,X)`! Why? Programs constantly need to glide across a memory block (a buffer) of up to 256 bytes—drawing one row of pixels, copying text, or scanning table columns—simply by placing a single base pointer in Zero Page and counting `Y` upward (`0, 1, 2, 3...`). Storing a whole array of 2-byte pointers inside precious 256-byte Zero Page for `(zp,X)` was far rarer.

Watch one subtle boundary difference too. In `(zp,X)`, adding `X` to `zp` stays strictly trapped inside Zero Page: if `zp` is `0xFE` and `X` is `4`, `0xFE + 4` wraps cleanly back around to `0x02`, never crossing into Page 1! By contrast, in `(zp),Y`, adding `Y` to the fetched 16-bit pointer *does* carry normally across memory pages—costing our familiar one extra clock tick whenever `Y` nudges the address onto the next page.

questions.prompt: Why did real-world 6502 programmers rely on indirect indexed (zp),Y far more heavily than indexed indirect (zp,X)?
choices: (zp,X) could only read numbers smaller than 128 and refused to load text characters.
Programs constantly walk through arrays, strings, and screen rows from one base pointer by stepping Y.
(zp,X) was removed from the 6502 silicon after Motorola's 1975 patent settlement.
(zp),Y finished in a single clock cycle while (zp,X) required twenty clock cycles per read.
questions.explanation: Stepping through a contiguous block of up to 256 bytes from a single Zero Page pointer with Y matched everyday tasks like copying strings, arrays, and screen lines far better than keeping large pointer tables in Zero Page.

questions.prompt: What happens if the addition inside (zp,X) exceeds 0xFF (such as 0xFE + 4), compared with adding Y to the final 16-bit pointer in (zp),Y?
choices: Both modes crash the processor immediately and force the user to reboot the computer.
Both modes wrap strictly inside Zero Page and can never touch addresses above 0x00FF.
(zp,X) wraps inside Zero Page without carrying, whereas (zp),Y carries normally into the next page.
(zp,X) carries into Page 1 (0x0102), whereas (zp),Y drops the carry and stays on the original page.
questions.explanation: Zero Page indexing in (zp,X) discards any carry so the lookup stays within 0x0000–0x00FF, while adding Y to the fetched 16-bit pointer in (zp),Y carries properly into the next memory page.

chunks.title: Conquering 64 Kilobytes—And Stepping Up to Page 1
chunks.content_markdown:
That completes the mystery of how a processor with tiny 8-bit index registers navigated a full 64-kilobyte universe! By parking changeable 16-bit **pointers** in **Zero Page**, MOS Technology gave programmers two sharply distinct tools: **indexed indirect `(zp,X)`** to pluck a specific bookmark from a table of pointers, and **indirect indexed `(zp),Y`** to stride rapidly across arrays, text buffers, and screen rows. Pair those two modes with 2-stage fetch/execute overlap, and the minimalist 6502 felt startlingly nimble.

We have now thoroughly explored Page 0 (`0x0000`–`0x00FF`), the 6502's beloved tool belt. Yet the very next 256-byte floor upstairs—**Page 1** (`0x0100`–`0x01FF`)—also holds a hardwired job built directly into the 6502's silicon! And as you might guess from seeing how minimalist 8-bit counters sometimes wrap around instead of carrying, those shortcuts can produce unforgettable surprises. Next, we climb up to Page 1 and inspect the 6502's most famous hardware bug.

questions.prompt: A game stores a single pointer in Zero Page pointing to the start of the current 40-character screen row and wants to copy all 40 characters quickly. Which mode fits best?
choices: Indexed indirect (zp,X), storing 40 separate two-byte pointers inside Zero Page for every letter.
Ordinary Zero Page addressing without pointers, because screen memory always lives inside 0x0000–0x00FF.
Indirect indexed (zp),Y, stepping Y from 0 to 39 after following the row's base pointer.
Big-endian addressing, because text rows must be read from high byte to low byte.
questions.explanation: Indirect indexed (zp),Y lets one 2-byte Zero Page pointer target any screen row in memory while register Y steps cleanly across characters 0 through 39.

questions.prompt: How did Zero Page indirect addressing reinforce the overall 6502 design philosophy?
choices: It required adding four bulky 16-bit index registers onto the silicon die.
It let lean 8-bit registers manipulate dynamic 16-bit addresses across 64 KB without bloating the chip.
It forced programmers to write every application entirely inside the first 256 bytes of RAM.
It replaced all memory chips with slow external tape drives to cut retail pricing.
questions.explanation: Keeping 16-bit pointers in Zero Page let the 6502 stay tiny with 8-bit registers X and Y while still offering flexible, fast access across all 65,536 memory locations.

sections.title: 6. The Page-1 Hardware Stack & the Indirect JMP Wraparound Bug
sections.summary: Examine how an 8-bit stack pointer hardwired the 6502's 256-byte hardware stack into Page 1 (0x0100–0x01FF)—trading recursion depth for compact speed—and dissect the famous indirect JMP page-boundary wraparound bug, where jumping through an address ending in hex xxFF such as 0x02FF fetches its high byte from 0x0200 instead of 0x0300.

chunks.title: Cafeteria Trays on Floor One: Why the Stack Lives in Page 1
chunks.content_markdown:
Every real computer program relies on reusable mini-programs called **subroutines**—for instance, a single routine that draws a letter on screen, called hundreds of times from different places. Each time a program jumps into a subroutine, the processor needs to remember where it left off so it can return afterward. To track nested calls cleanly, processors use a **stack**: a last-in, first-out pile just like a spring-loaded tower of cafeteria trays, where you always **push** a new tray onto the top and **pull** the topmost tray off first.

Motorola's 6800 dedicated a full 16-bit stack pointer register so programmers could park the stack anywhere in memory. The minimalist 6502, however, trimmed its stack pointer (`S`) down to just **8 bits** to save silicon! Since an 8-bit number only selects 256 slots (`0x00` to `0xFF`), the 6502 hardwired the high byte of every stack address to `0x01`, permanently fixing its **Page-1 hardware stack** at addresses `0x0100` through `0x01FF`.

questions.prompt: Why does a microprocessor rely on a last-in, first-out stack when calling nested subroutines?
choices: So the newest saved return address pulls off first, unwinding nested calls cleanly.
So the oldest variable ever created is always erased before the newest instruction finishes running.
So every subroutine can skip using accumulator A and write directly to the video screen.
So the processor can execute all subroutines in alphabetical order regardless of program flow.
questions.explanation: Like cafeteria trays, nested subroutine calls finish in reverse order of how they started, so pushing return addresses onto a last-in, first-out stack ensures each return lands at the exact right spot.

questions.prompt: Why is the 6502's hardware stack permanently fixed at memory addresses 0x0100 through 0x01FF?
choices: Memory chips manufactured in 1975 could only hold temporary return addresses inside Page 1.
Because stack pointer S is only 8 bits wide, the 6502 hardwires the stack's high address byte to 0x01.
Page 0 was completely empty and unusable, forcing MOS Technology to shift all variables upward.
Motorola held an exclusive patent forbidding any rival chip from placing a stack above 0x0200.
questions.explanation: Trimming S to 8 bits saved transistors while limiting it to 256 offsets (0x00–0xFF), so the hardware automatically prepended 0x01 to anchor the stack in Page 1.

chunks.title: Living Inside 256 Bytes: Speed vs. Stack Ceiling
chunks.content_markdown:
Inside the **Page-1 hardware stack** (`0x0100`–`0x01FF`), the 6502 builds its pile *downward*, starting from the ceiling at `0x01FF` and stepping toward `0x0100`. Pushing a byte—such as saving accumulator `A` or storing a 2-byte return address when calling a subroutine—writes into `0x0100 + S` and subtracts 1 from `S`. Pulling a byte adds 1 to `S` and reads it back. Updating only an 8-bit pointer keeps subroutine calls, temporary saves, and urgent hardware **interrupts** (signals pausing normal code to handle a keypress or timer) brisk and compact.

Yet that hard 256-byte limit carried a memorable trade-off. Hand-written assembly programs—code written directly in raw processor instructions—rarely nested more than a dozen subroutines deep, so 256 bytes felt spacious; clever coders even borrowed unused lower Page-1 slots as scratch space! High-level languages like C or Pascal, however, love deep recursive calls (subroutines repeatedly calling themselves) and piling local variables onto the stack. Push past `0x0100` on a 6502, and `S` silently wraps right back to `0x01FF`, clobbering older return bookmarks!

questions.prompt: As bytes are pushed onto the 6502's Page-1 hardware stack, how does stack pointer S move?
choices: It counts upward starting at 0x0100 and automatically expands into Page 2 once full.
It stays locked permanently at 0x0180 while shifting every older byte down by one slot.
It counts downward from 0xFF toward 0x00 inside Page 1, subtracting 1 after each push.
It alternates between even addresses in Page 1 and odd addresses in Zero Page.
questions.explanation: The 6502's stack grows downward from 0x01FF toward 0x0100: each push stores a byte at 0x0100 + S and decrements S, while each pull increments S first and reads back.

questions.prompt: What happens on the 6502 if a deeply nested program pushes more than 256 bytes onto the Page-1 hardware stack?
choices: The processor automatically reallocates a fresh 1,024-byte stack in Page 4 to prevent errors.
The stack spills safely downward into Zero Page and converts the top variables into return addresses.
The 8-bit stack pointer wraps around inside Page 1, silently overwriting older stack entries.
The on-chip clock generator halts and flashes a warning code across the data pins.
questions.explanation: Because the high byte is hardwired to 0x01 and S is only 8 bits wide, decrementing S past 0x00 wraps back to 0xFF (0x01FF), silently overwriting older entries on Page 1.

chunks.title: The Famous Silicon Quirk: Jumping Through 0x02FF
chunks.content_markdown:
That exact same 8-bit shortcut—counting only the low byte without carrying into the high byte—also produced the 6502's most legendary hardware bug! Alongside ordinary jumps to fixed locations, the 6502 includes an **indirect jump**, written `JMP (addr)`. Just like looking up a forwarding address, `JMP (addr)` reads a 2-byte little-endian **pointer** stored at `addr` and `addr + 1`, then leaps to that destination address. Operating systems loved indirect jumps because updating one pointer redirected programs seamlessly to newer system routines.

Watch what goes wrong if you park that pointer right on a page edge—at **`0x02FF`**, executing `JMP (0x02FF)`! First, the 6502 reads the destination's low byte from `0x02FF`. Next, to fetch the high byte, its minimalist address counter adds `1` *only to the low byte* (`0xFF + 1` becomes `0x00`) without carrying into the high byte `0x02`! Instead of reading the high byte from **`0x0300`**, the 6502 leaps backward to **`0x0200`**, assembling a completely mangled destination address!

questions.prompt: Why did 6502 operating systems and programmers use the indirect JMP (addr) instruction?
choices: It let programs double the size of the Page-1 hardware stack during long calculations.
It jumped directly to Zero Page while automatically clearing accumulator A and register X.
It allowed the processor to execute two different subroutines at the same instant.
It jumped through a changeable memory pointer so routines could move without rewriting calling code.
questions.explanation: An indirect jump reads a 2-byte pointer from memory and jumps to the address stored there, making flexible jump tables and patchable system hooks easy to build.

questions.prompt: On the original NMOS 6502, where does JMP (0x02FF) actually fetch the low and high bytes of its jump destination?
choices: Low byte from 0x02FF and high byte from 0x0300, crossing cleanly into Page 3.
Low byte from 0x0300 and high byte from 0x02FF, reversing little-endian order.
Low byte from 0x02FF and high byte from 0x0200, wrapping back to the start of Page 2.
Low byte from 0x02FE and high byte from 0x02FF, stepping backward to avoid Page 3.
questions.explanation: Because the original 6502 increments only the low byte of the indirect pointer address without propagating a carry, JMP (0x02FF) fetches its low byte from 0x02FF and its high byte from 0x0200 instead of 0x0300.

chunks.title: Why Page-Boundary Wraparound Survived—And How Coders Dodged It
chunks.content_markdown:
Engineers call this quirk **page-boundary wraparound**: whenever an 8-bit low-byte counter rolls over from `0xFF` to `0x00` without adding a carry of `1` to the high byte, the address loops right back to the start of the *same* 256-byte page instead of crossing into the next page. On the original NMOS 6502, **page-boundary wraparound** strikes any indirect `JMP` whose pointer starts at an address ending in `hex xxFF`—such as `0x02FF`, `0x10FF`, or `0x45FF`.

Why didn't MOS Technology immediately stop the presses and fix the silicon? Remember our 3,510-transistor budget! Adding carry-propagation logic and an extra fix-up cycle specifically for rare edge-case indirect jumps would have added transistors and complexity to a razor-tight die. Instead, MOS Technology documented the quirk and programmers adopted a simple golden rule: never align an indirect `JMP` pointer on a `hex xxFF` byte! Years later, Bill Mensch's low-power CMOS successor (the 65C02) finally spent an extra clock tick to fix the carry properly.

questions.prompt: What does page-boundary wraparound describe in the original 6502's indirect JMP bug?
choices: A jump destination automatically relocating itself into Zero Page whenever memory runs low.
Incrementing 0xFF rolls to 0x00 without carrying 1, looping back to the same page's start.
A program counter stepping backward through memory whenever a subroutine runs longer than 256 bytes.
A memory chip physically overheating at the corner of a silicon wafer during high-speed jumps.
questions.explanation: Page-boundary wraparound occurs when incrementing 0xFF yields 0x00 without adding a carry to the high byte, wrapping back to byte 0x00 of the current 256-byte page.

questions.prompt: Which of these indirect jump instructions triggers the original NMOS 6502 page-boundary wraparound bug?
choices: JMP (0x1000), because its low byte begins cleanly at zero.
JMP (0x10FE), because its two pointer bytes occupy 0x10FE and 0x10FF on Page 0x10.
JMP (0x1080), because 0x80 sits exactly halfway across Page 0x10.
JMP (0x10FF), because its pointer begins on the final byte of Page 0x10.
questions.explanation: Any indirect JMP pointer starting at an address ending in hex xxFF—like 0x10FF—triggers the bug, fetching its high byte from 0x1000 instead of 0x1100; 0x10FE safely uses 0x10FE and 0x10FF.

chunks.title: From Bare Silicon to Six World-Changing Machines
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back and admire the unity of what we have uncovered across Sections 1 through 6. Every signature feature—and every famous quirk—of the MOS Technology 6502 flows from one relentless principle: trim silicon ruthlessly to hit 25 dollars, then wring dazzling speed out of every remaining transistor. That philosophy produced 3,510 depletion-mode NMOS switches, little-endian 2-stage fetch/execute overlap, Zero Page pseudo-registers, `(zp,X)` and `(zp),Y` indirect pointers, the compact **Page-1 hardware stack**, and even the quirky `hex xxFF` **page-boundary wraparound** bug.

Yet brilliant silicon alone does not change history—computers do! Because the 6502 was astonishingly cheap, fast, and easy to wire up, imaginative designers across three continents built landmark home computers and game consoles around it. Over our final four sections, we explore six unforgettable 6502 platforms—beginning in a California garage where one gifted engineer turned a 25-dollar WESCON bargain into the Apple II.

questions.prompt: What shared engineering root connects both the fixed Page-1 hardware stack and the indirect JMP page-boundary wraparound bug?
choices: Both arose from MOS Technology's deliberate use of lean 8-bit address counters to minimize transistors.
Both were intentional anti-piracy traps added at Motorola's request during the 1976 lawsuit settlement.
Both happened only when programmers forgot to attach an external two-phase clock generator chip.
Both resulted from random microscopic dust particles landing on glass photomasks in Pennsylvania.
questions.explanation: Using compact 8-bit address counters without full 16-bit carry hardware kept the 6502 tiny and affordable, yielding both the fixed 256-byte Page-1 stack and the indirect JMP wraparound quirk.
